title: The uneven rise of AI-generated web content
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:The uneven rise of AI-generated web content
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:In less than five years, generative artificial intelligence (AI) has dramatically reshaped the public-facing web. Using a sample of more than 5 million crawlable webpages, we demonstrate that the share containing AI-generated text has increased precipitously, but unevenly. Our analyses reveal substantial differences in AI composition across language and domain categories (e.g., .edu, .com, or .gov). A higher fraction of English-language webpages contain AI-generated text compared to pages in other languages, and prevalence is substantially lower on .gov and .edu domains compared to .com. These distinctions persist even after accounting for compositional effects. We also find heterogeneity based on a page's position in the connectivity structure of the web. AI-generated text is most common and has increased most rapidly in pages that are the least central in the graph, which drives much of the overall growth in AI-generated text. A slower increase has taken place for more central pages, with the most central tier emerging as the least likely to contain AI-generated text. Methodologically, we use multiple AI detection tools, and generate estimates using a Bayesian hierarchical model that incorporates corrections for the detectors' statistical properties (both false positives and false negatives) and allows for different detector performance across groups, while propagating uncertainty in detector error rates into prevalence estimates. Our work suggests that AI is a prominent, but varied, contributor to public information and internet-based communication.

report.summary: A 5-million-page crawl finds AI-generated text spreading fast across the web but very unevenly, concentrated in English, .com, and peripheral pages.
report.background: Since ChatGPT's late-2022 launch, generative models have made it cheap to mass-produce articles, product descriptions, SEO spam and forum posts. Researchers, search engines and AI labs have all suspected the public web is filling with synthetic text, but hard numbers were scarce: AI-text detectors are imperfect, error rates vary by domain and language, and small samples rarely capture the web's structural diversity. Earlier work looked at narrow slices such as academic abstracts, Amazon reviews or news sites. This paper attempts a broader measurement, combining a large multi-domain crawl with several detectors and a statistical model that corrects for false positives and false negatives rather than trusting any single classifier. The question matters because the web is both the public information commons and the main training corpus for future models — so its composition directly shapes what the next generation of AI systems learns, and what humans and search engines read.
key_points: Scale and method: the authors analysed more than 5 million crawlable webpages using several AI-text detectors at once. Rather than trusting any single classifier, they built a Bayesian hierarchical model that corrects for detectors' false positives and false negatives, allows detector accuracy to differ across groups of pages, and carries that uncertainty through to the final prevalence estimates.

Language gap: a higher fraction of English-language pages contain AI-generated text than pages in other languages. The authors report that this difference holds even after accounting for compositional effects — that is, it is not simply an artefact of English pages being more likely to belong to domains where AI text is common.

Domain gap: prevalence is substantially lower on .gov and .edu domains than on .com. Government and university pages, which tend to be institutional and reviewed, look measurably more human-written than commercial pages, again after controlling for other characteristics of the pages sampled.

Position in the web graph matters: AI-generated text is most common, and has grown fastest, on pages that are least central in the web's link connectivity structure. This long tail drives most of the overall growth, while the most central, heavily linked tier is the least likely of all to contain AI-generated text.

The rise is steep but recent: within less than five years, the share of crawled pages containing AI-generated text rose sharply, suggesting generative AI has become a prominent — if unevenly distributed — contributor to public information and internet-based communication.
report.impact: The findings reframe the AI-content debate from 'is the web being flooded?' to 'where, exactly?' For AI developers, the concentration in low-centrality English .com pages is a data-quality warning: training crawls will absorb a growing amount of synthetic text precisely where filtering is weakest, raising model-collapse and benchmark-contamination risks and arguing for provenance metadata and better corpus curation. For the AI industry, uneven penetration means detection tools, watermarking and content-credential standards need language- and domain-aware calibration, not one global accuracy number. For regular users, search results and long-tail informational pages are the likeliest to be machine-written, while government and education sites remain comparatively human-sourced — a useful heuristic for judging trust, and a reminder that 'the internet' is no longer a single, uniform information environment.
report.tools: To follow up, Common Crawl and the Web Data Commons host-level graph provide comparable crawl and link data; open-source detectors such as Binoculars, DetectGPT/Fast-DetectGPT and GPTZero's public API let you experiment with detection; PyMC or Stan are suitable for building the kind of Bayesian hierarchical correction used here; FastAPI plus a small pipeline can replicate prevalence estimation on your own domain sample; and C2PA Content Credentials are worth watching as a provenance-based alternative to post-hoc detection.
